title: THE DEMONS BEGGED JESUS FOR PERMISSION. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE PIGS TERRIFIED THE TOWN.
paragraphs: THE DEMONS BEGGED JESUS FOR PERMISSION. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE PIGS TERRIFIED THE TOWN.
They had chained the man, abandoned him among the tombs, and learned to live with his screams. Then Jesus stepped onto the shore—and suddenly the demons were the ones begging.
There is something almost unbearable about the scene in Mark 5.
Before Jesus arrived, everyone was afraid of the man.
After Jesus arrived, even the demons were afraid of Jesus.
And by the end of the story, the townspeople were afraid too.
But strangely, they were not most frightened by the demons.
They were frightened by what happened when Jesus took authority over them.
That detail should make us uncomfortable.
Because this story is not merely about a demonized man, two thousand pigs, and a frightened town somewhere on the eastern side of the Sea of Galilee.
It is about what happens when Jesus walks into territory where darkness has been allowed to stay for a very long time.
And before you finish reading, you may discover something disturbing:
Sometimes we become so accustomed to our chains that freedom feels more frightening than captivity.

Mark tells us that Jesus and His disciples crossed the sea and entered the region of the Gerasenes. The manuscript tradition contains geographical variants such as “Gadarenes” and “Gergesenes,” but the central event is unmistakable: Jesus entered predominantly Gentile territory, where a large herd of pigs was being kept.
Then a man came toward Him.
Not from a house.
Not from a synagogue.
From the tombs.
Mark describes a human being who had become almost unrecognizable beneath his torment.
People had tried restraining him with shackles and chains.
He broke them.
No one could subdue him.
Night and day he wandered among the tombs and mountains, screaming and cutting himself with stones.
Think about that.
Somebody once knew his childhood laugh.
Somebody may have remembered what his face looked like before torment hollowed it out.
Perhaps somebody once ate dinner beside him.
Perhaps someone had once called him son, brother, neighbor, friend.
Now people knew him by what was wrong with him.
The dangerous one.
The possessed one.
The man in the cemetery.
Isn't that what brokenness so often does?
It slowly replaces your name with your wound.
Addict.
Failure.
Adulterer.
Divorced.
Unclean.
Crazy.
Hopeless.
Backslider.
Porn addict.
Drunk.
Fraud.
Hypocrite.
And after hearing the label long enough, you begin answering to it.
But Jesus crossed a stormy sea for a man everyone else had apparently learned to avoid.
That matters.
Because there are people reading this who secretly believe they have gone too far.
You know how to smile in photographs.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know how to sit in church.
But there are tombs inside you nobody sees.
Memories you revisit at 2:00 in the morning.
Habits you promised God you would stop.
Shame you keep deleting from your browser but cannot delete from your conscience.
Anger you disguise as strength.
Pain you disguise as humor.
Spiritual exhaustion you disguise as being “busy.”
Maybe nobody hears you screaming because you learned how to scream silently.
Mark 5 is for people who have started wondering whether Jesus still comes looking for people like that.
He does.
When the tormented man saw Jesus from a distance, something extraordinary happened.
He ran toward Him.
The Greek text says:
καὶ προσκύνησεν αὐτῷ — kai prosekynēsen autō
He fell before Him.
Then the voice coming from this tormented man cried out and identified Jesus:
Ἰησοῦ υἱὲ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου — Iēsou huie tou Theou tou Hypsistou
“Jesus, Son of the Most High God.”
Do not miss the terrifying irony.
The demons knew who Jesus was.
Recognition is not salvation.
You can possess correct theology about Jesus without belonging to Jesus.
James later writes that even the demons believe—and shudder.
That should disturb every person who has confused familiarity with Christianity for surrender to Christ.
Knowing Christian language is not the same as knowing Christ.
Owning a Bible is not repentance.
Posting Scripture is not repentance.
Attending church is not repentance.
Calling Jesus “Lord” while deliberately protecting the sin He commands you to surrender is not discipleship.
The demons in Mark 5 possessed information about Jesus.
What they did not possess was authority over Jesus.
Jesus commanded the unclean spirit to come out.
Then came the question:
“What is your name?”
The answer has echoed for nearly two thousand years.
Λεγιὼν ὄνομά μοι, ὅτι πολλοί ἐσμεν.
Legiōn onoma moi, hoti polloi esmen.
“My name is Legion, for we are many.”

“Legion” was a Roman military term associated with a massive body of soldiers. The text does not require us to calculate an exact number of demons from the Roman military establishment. The point is overwhelming multiplicity.
Many.
This man was catastrophically oppressed.
Yet notice something astonishing.
There may have been many of them.
There was only one Jesus.
And nobody reading Mark's account is left wondering who possessed the authority.
The demons began begging Him.
Read that again.
The creatures terrorizing the man were terrified before Christ.
They pleaded not to be sent away from the region. A large herd of pigs was feeding nearby, and the spirits begged Jesus to send them into the animals.
Then Mark records one of the most chilling sentences in the passage.
Jesus permitted them.
The Greek wording is devastating in its simplicity:
καὶ ἐπέτρεψεν αὐτοῖς — kai epetrepsen autois
“He permitted them.”
Permission.
The demons did not negotiate as equals.
They did not overpower Christ.
Jesus did not barely survive a cosmic wrestling match.
They begged.
He permitted.
They obeyed.
This is one reason Christians must never build a fascination with demons that becomes greater than their confidence in Christ.
Scripture does not present Jesus trembling before Legion.
Legion trembles before Jesus.
Then the unclean spirits entered the pigs.
And suddenly the hillside erupted.
About two thousand animals stampeded down the steep bank into the sea and drowned.
Imagine the sound.
Thousands of hooves pounding earth.
Animals screaming.
Herdsmen shouting.
Dust exploding upward.
Then the violent rush toward the water.
And afterward...
silence.
The herdsmen ran.
News spread through the surrounding countryside.
People rushed toward Jesus.
And when they arrived, they saw something that should have caused celebration.
The man.
But not the man they remembered.
Mark says he was:
καθήμενον ἱματισμένον καὶ σωφρονοῦντα
Sitting.
Clothed.
And in his right mind.
The man who could not be restrained was sitting peacefully.
The man who had lived naked among graves was clothed.
The mind that had been tormented was restored.
The cemetery had lost its prisoner.
This should have become a worship service.
Someone should have shouted.
Someone should have embraced him.
Someone should have fallen at Jesus' feet and said, “If You can do that for him, have mercy on me too.”
Instead, Mark says:
καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν — kai ephobēthēsan
“And they were afraid.”
Then witnesses explained what had happened to the man—and what had happened to the pigs.
And the townspeople made their decision.
They begged Jesus to leave.
Don't rush past that.
Earlier, the demons begged Jesus.
Now the townspeople begged Jesus.
The demons begged for permission to enter the pigs.
The people begged Jesus to leave their region.
That may be one of the saddest scenes in the Gospel of Mark.
The delivered man wanted Jesus close.
The town wanted Jesus gone.
Why?

Scripture explicitly says they were afraid. The destruction of such an enormous herd also plainly represented a severe material loss, although we should be careful not to claim that Mark explicitly says money was their sole motive.
But the contrast forces a haunting question.
What happens when the presence of Jesus disrupts the life we have become comfortable living?
Everyone likes the idea of Jesus bringing peace.
Until His peace requires surrender.
Everyone likes freedom.
Until freedom threatens an idol.
Everyone wants revival.
Until revival enters the bank account.
The bedroom.
The browser history.
The relationship.
The pride.
The secret habit.
The business practice.
The resentment.
The identity we built without God.
We want Jesus to calm our storms.
But sometimes we do not want Him touching our pigs.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story stops being ancient.
Maybe your “pigs” are not literal possessions.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is pornography you keep renaming “a struggle” because calling it sin would demand repentance.
Maybe it is bitterness you have protected so long that forgiveness feels like betrayal.
Maybe it is money.
Status.
Attention.
Sexual sin.
Pride.
Approval.
A hidden second life.
Maybe you love Jesus—as long as Jesus does not walk into that room.
But Christ does not come merely to decorate our captivity with religious language.
He comes as Lord.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping you become a slightly improved version of the person chained among the tombs.
It is death and resurrection.
Repentance and grace.
Forgiveness and transformation.
The old passing away.
The captive becoming free.
And that freedom has a cost infinitely greater than a herd of pigs.
Because Mark 5 quietly points us toward something even greater.
Jesus crossed the sea to rescue a tormented man.
Eventually Jesus would go toward another place associated with death.
A cross.
And this time, there would be no escaping the cost.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God would give Himself for sinners.
Jesus did not die because demons defeated Him.
He willingly laid down His life.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose bodily from the grave.
The Christian hope is not merely that Jesus can improve damaged people.
It is that the crucified and risen Christ saves sinners.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that repentant sinners can be forgiven.
That is why your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your adultery does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice what happened next.
As Jesus prepared to leave, the formerly demonized man began begging Him.
Another plea.
Three scenes of begging.
Demons begged.
Townspeople begged.
The delivered man begged.
But his request was different.
He wanted to be with Jesus.
Can you blame him?
Jesus was perhaps the first Person in a very long time who looked at him and saw something worth rescuing.
The town had chains for him.
Jesus had mercy.
The town pushed him toward the tombs.
Jesus restored him to life.
So the man wanted into the boat.
But Jesus said no.
Not because He rejected him.
Because He commissioned him.
“Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you and how He has had mercy on you.”
Home.
Sometimes the hardest mission field is home.
Go back to the people who remember what you were.
Go back where everyone knows the scandal.
Go back where they remember the screaming.
Go back where your reputation arrives before you do.
And tell them about mercy.
The man obeyed.
Mark says he went throughout the Decapolis—the “Ten Cities”—proclaiming what Jesus had done for him.
Think about the transformation.
The mouth that had screamed among tombs now proclaimed mercy among cities.
The man once controlled by a legion became a witness for Jesus.
The person everyone feared became the person telling everyone what Christ had done.
That is Gospel transformation.
Jesus did not merely silence his torment.
He gave his story a new ending.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else today.
You are not required to pretend your past never happened.
Bring it to Christ.
Repent honestly.
Receive His mercy by faith.
Then let the scars point toward the Savior.
Maybe the very chapter you wish you could tear from your life will someday become the chapter through which another broken person realizes there is hope.
Peter denied Christ and became a preacher of Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle proclaiming Christ.
The Gerasene man lived among tombs and became a messenger of mercy.
This is what grace does.
It does not call darkness light.
It enters darkness and brings people into light.
So I want to ask you something more personal than whether you enjoyed this article.
What are you asking Jesus to do?
And what are you quietly asking Him not to touch?
Because eventually every heart in Mark 5 reveals itself by what it begs Jesus for.
The demons wanted somewhere else to go.
The town wanted Jesus to go.
The restored man wanted to go with Jesus.
Which prayer sounds most like yours?
Do not answer quickly.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has exposed something while you were reading.
Something hidden.
Something you keep defending.
Something that has been chaining you internally while everyone around you assumes you are fine.
Bring it into the light.
Christ is not calling you to perform.
He is calling you to repent and believe.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes a simple public confession of need becomes the moment we stop pretending.

And if Christ has already brought you through something people thought would destroy you, do not hide the testimony. Tell us what Jesus did. Someone reading the comments may be standing near the tomb you once escaped.
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Someone you went to school with.
A relative.
A coworker.
A believer who has drifted.
A person who has never trusted Christ.
You may never know who stops scrolling tonight because you shared something that reminded them Jesus still receives sinners.
It cannot.
Not because giving money earns salvation. It never will.
Christ purchased salvation; we do not.
But one practical way to glorify God with the resources He entrusts to us is to support faithful Gospel work so that biblical content and discipleship resources can continue reaching people.
The demons knew His identity.
The town witnessed His power.
The delivered man experienced His mercy.
Only one of them wanted to stay with Jesus.
You can admire Christ and still resist Him.
You can fear Christ and still send Him away.
You can know facts about Christ and still remain unsurrendered.
The question is not merely whether Jesus has come near.
The question is what you will do now that He has.
The man who woke among tombs walked home carrying a testimony.
And somewhere between the cemetery and his front door, the scandal everyone remembered became the evidence of a mercy nobody could deny.
The town remembered the man who lived among the dead; Jesus saw the messenger who was about to tell cities where life could be found.
